title: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
titleZh: Apple's git still trusts the compromised eMudhra certificates
author: galadran
relevanceReason: 命中 3 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Apple was notified of the eMudhra incident on 17th October. As of 28th October, the developer tools Apple ships with macOS, including git, curl and python3, still trust the compromised certificates.
Worse, macOS 27.2, released on 26th October, did not fix the issue and undid the workaround that users had applied by hand, leaving them vulnerable again.
Meanwhile, dozens of other projects, many run by volunteers, shipped fixes days ago.

comments.author: chrisweekly
comments.textRawHtml:
Right, so it's not just git, it's a bunch of system-provided utilities; macOS trusts bad certs, and these utils that trust the OS are affected. I use homebrew for my git and curl but haven't yet checked to confirm whether that matters here. 
Kind of outrageous that Apple's guidance is to edit the cert chain manually, and to expect that subsequent OS updates may revert your mitigation, reintroducing the vulnerability (as happened at least once so far).

children.textRawHtml:
What kind of psychopath ships 100 distinct container images? I mean, maybe if you’re talking about all of Netflix or something, but… I suspect even they have base images that they use as a starting point.

There’s very little actually running in a docker container. ca-certs may actually be an exceptional case though, since it’s not code that’s running but a kind of data.

It’s not like if you use an Ubuntu image for a node.js app that you get PHP too and have the PHP vulnerability present in your web app.

children.author: mikepurvis
children.textRawHtml:
I think the number one thing that bites a lot of container workflows is when you have a separate "base image" build that depends on external, mutable package sources using tools that don't support locking, such as apt.

This gets worse for each additional such layer, for example if you start from ubuntu:whatever and have a system deps layer, then an application deps layer, then static assets, then your app's code. Unless you think about it upfront when designing the pipeline, it can be challenging to trace all that state backwards and figure out how to safely re-build thing-from-x-weeks ago but with a single unsafe package bumped forward.

Every shop with competent devops people present should be set up for this, but it usually doesn't come for free.
